narrative:
The model predicted a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 25.5, it sits well below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model. Your first-year and third-year grades in law school also mattered, but in opposite ways. Your third-year performance pulled the prediction toward failure because you ranked in the 3rd decile compared with an average around the 6th decile for accepted students. In contrast, your undergraduate GPA of 2.8 actually worked in your favor by slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure, though not enough to overcome the other signals.

Family income, full-time status, gender, and race played no role in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your standardized test performance and strengthening your academic record in law school. Retaking the LSAT and aiming for a significantly higher score, combined with consistent top-decile grades, would most directly address the factors that led to this rejection. Consider reapplying once those improvements are reflected in your record.
